Xanthippe.x:
also (incorrectly) Xantippe, late 16c., spouse of Socrates (5c. B.C.E.), the prototype of the quarrelsome, nagging wife. The name is related to the masc. proper name Xanthippos, a compound of xanthos "yellow" (see xantho-) + hippos "horse" (from PIE root *ekwo- "horse").
Historically, little is known of her. Xenophon's Symposium, where Socrates is asked why he married the most intractable woman ever, reputation for subsequent millennia as a shrew. The philosopher's answer: “I observe that men who wish to become expert horsemen do not get the most docile horses but rather those that are high-mettled, believing that if they can manage this kind, they will easily handle any other."

Xerxes.x: king of Persia who reigned 486-465 B.C.E., Greek Xerxes, from Old Persian Xšayaršan, literally "male (i.e. 'hero') among kings," from Xšaya- "to rule over" (see shah) + aršan "male, man, hero." The Hebrew rendition was Ahashwerosh, Ahashresh.

xenia.x: city in Ohio, from Greek xenia "hospitality, rights of a guest, friendly relation with strangers," literally "state of a guest," from xenos "guest" (from PIE root *ghos-ti- "stranger, guest, host"). Founded 1803 and named by vote of a town meeting, on suggestion of the Rev. Robert Armstrong, to imply friendliness and hospitality.

xenon.x: heavy, inert gaseous element, 1898, from Greek xenon, neuter of xenos "foreign, strange" (from PIE root *ghos-ti- "stranger, guest, host"); coined by its co-discoverer, Scottish chemist Sir William Ramsay (1852-1916). Compare krypton (kryptos "hidden") neon (neos "new"), argon (argos "idle") all allied and named during the same rush of discovery, but the names perhaps randomly distributed, as no suggestion is made that xenon is stranger or argon lazier than the others.

xenophobia.x:
"fear or hatred of strangers or what is foreign," 1880, London Daily News, April 12, in which it is coupled with xenomania, in reference to English attitudes toward the French:
See xeno- "foreign, strange" + -phobia "fear." It was infrequent in 1890s publications but more common from 1903, influenced by or from French xénophobie (by 1901), xénophobe. Earlier (c. 1884) it meant what now is meant by agoraphobia.

xerography.x: "photographic reduplication without liquid developers," 1948, from Greek xeros "dry" (see xero-) + -ography as in photography. Related: Xerographic.

xylophone.x: musical instrument consisting of a graduated series of wooden bars, sounded by hand-held wooden hammers, 1866, coined from Greek elements: xylon "wood" (see xylo-) + phōnē "a sound" (from PIE root *bha- (2) "to speak, tell, say"). In early accounts occasionally Englished as music-sticks. Related: Xylophonist.

xyster.x: "surgical instrument for scraping bones," 1680s, from Greek xyster "a graving tool," from xyein "to scrape." Beekes compare Sanskrit ksnauti "to grind, whet, rub," Lithuanian skusti "to shave, plane." Perhaps from a PIE *kes- "to scrape."

xanthosis.x: in pathology, "yellowish discoloration," 1857, Modern Latin, from Greek xanthos (see xantho-) + -osis.

xenolith.x: 1894, in geology, "piece of rock in an igneous mass different from the rest," and considered to have been picked up by it; by 1839 in German, from xeno- "foreign, strange" + -lith "stone."

xi.x: fourteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, by early 15c. in English.

xeroderma.x: "condition of dry and harsh skin," 1848, from xero- + derma.

Xmas.x:
"Christmas," by 1551, X'temmas, wherein the X is an abbreviation for Christ in Christmas, English letter X being identical in form (but not sound signification) to Greek chi, the first letter of Greek Khristos "Christ" (see Christ).
The earlier way to abbreviate the word in English was Xp- or Xr- (corresponding to the "Chr-" in Greek Χριστος), and the form Xres mæsse for "Christmas" appears in the "Anglo-Saxon Chronicle" (c. 1100).

xanthic.x: "tending toward a yellow color," 1817, in chemistry, of compounds producing yellowish substances, from French xanthique, from Greek xanthos "yellow" (see xantho-).

Xanadu.x: Mongol city founded by Kublai Khan, 1620s, Englished form of Shang-tu. The sense of "dream place of magnificence and luxury" derives from Coleridge's poem (1816).

xiphias.x: genus of swordfish, 1660s, from Greek xiphias "swordfish," from xiphos "a sword" (see xiphoid). Related: Xiphioid.

X-ray.x:
1896, X-rays, translation of German X-strahlen, from X, algebraic symbol for an unknown quantity, + Strahl (plural Strahlen) "beam, ray." Coined 1895 by German scientist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen (1845-1923), who discovered the rays, to suggest their exact nature was unknown.
As a verb by 1899. The meaning "image made using X-rays" is from 1934, earlier in this sense was X-radiograph (1899). Related: X-rayed. X-ray eyes, able to see through anything, is by 1896.

xantho-.x:
before vowels xanth-, word-forming element of Greek origin, meaning "yellow," from Greek xanthos "yellow" of various shades; used especially of hair and horses, a word of unknown origin.
The element was used in English from mid-19c., chiefly in forming scientific words such as xanthein (1857) "soluble yellow coloring matter in flowers," xanthophyll (1838) "yellow coloring matter in autumn leaves." Also T.H. Huxley's Xanthochroi (1867) "blond, light-skinned races of Europe" (with ōkhros "pale").

Xerox.x: 1952, trademark taken out by Haloid Co. of Rochester, N.Y., for a copying device, from xerography. The verb is attested by 1965, from the noun, despite strenuous objection from the Xerox copyright department. Related: Xeroxed; Xeroxing.

Xeres.x: Andalusian town (modern Jerez) famous for its wine; see sherry. For first letter, see xebec.

Xhosa.x: South African Bantu people, 1801, their self-designation. Also their language.

xebec.x: "small three-masted vessel," favored by Barbary corsairs but also used in Mediterranean trade, by 1745, from French chébec, from Italian sciabecco, ultimately from Arabic shabbak "a small warship." Altered by influence of cognate Spanish xabeque, which shows the old way of representing the Spanish sound now spelled -j-.

xeno-.x:
before vowels, xen-, word-forming element of Greek origin meaning "strange, foreign; stranger, foreigner," from Greek xenos "a guest, stranger, foreigner, refugee, guest-friend, one entitled to hospitality," cognate with Latin hostis, from PIE root *ghos-ti- "stranger, guest, host." "The term was politely used of any one whose name was unknown" [Liddell & Scott].
As an element in English, used from late 19c., at first in sciences, later in politics.

xeric.x: "having little moisture, very dry," 1926; see xero- + -ic.

xero-.x:
before vowels, xer-, word-forming element of Greek origin used from mid-129c. in scientific and technical terms, meaning "dry," from Greek xero-, combining form of xēros "dry, arid, withered."
This is reconstructed in Watkins, etc., to be from PIE root *ksero- "dry" (source also of Latin serenus "clear, unclouded," serescere "become dry;" Greek xeron "dry land;" Old High German serawen, German serben "to dry out").

xylem.x:
"woody tissue in higher plants," 1870, from German Xylem, coined from Greek xylon "wood" (see xylo-).
 Naegeli has divided the tissues of the vascular bundles into two groups. These are separated by the cambium, and are named Phloem and Xylem ; the Xylem part being the wood proper, while the Phloem is in general considered as part of the bark. [Monthly Microscopical Journal, March 1870]

xylo-.x:
before vowels xyl-, word forming element of Greek origin meaning "wood," from Greek xylon "wood cut and ready for use, firewood, timber; piece of wood; stocks, a plank, beam, or bench," in New Testament, "the Cross," a word of uncertain origin.
It seems to correspond with Lithuanian šulas "post, pole, stave," Russian šulo "garden-pole," Serbo-Croatian šulj "block," Old High German sul "style, pole," Gothic sauls "pillar," but the exact relationship is unclear, and Beekes asks, "Was the word taken from a non-IE substrate language?"
In English the element was used mostly from mid-19c. in forming scientific and technical terms. Blount (1656) has xylopolist "wood-monger, seller of timber."

xenial.x: "pertaining to hospitality," especially in reference to the guest-host relationship in Greek antiquity, 1834, from Greek xenia (see Xenia) + -al (1). Related: Xenially.

xylene.x: volatile colorless hydrocarbon obtained from wood spirits, 1850, from Greek xylon "wood" (see xylo-) + -ene, hydrocarbon suffix.

xerasia.x: "excessive dryness of hair," 1706, medical Latin, from Greek xerasia "dryness," from xeros "dry, withered" (see xero-).

xerosis.x: "xeroderma; dry, harsh skin," 1890, Modern Latin, from Greek xerosis, from xeros "dry" (see xero-) + -osis.

xerotic.x: in anatomy, "characterized by dryness," by 1868, from stem of xero- + -ic.

xiphoid.x: in anatomy, "sword-shaped, resembling a sword," 1746, with -oid + Greek xiphos "a sword," a word of unknown origin (Klein suggests a Semitic source and compares Hebrew sayif, Arabic sayf).

xanthous.x: 1826, "fair-haired and light-complexioned," from Greek xanthos "yellow," a word of unknown origin (see xantho-). Xanthous also was used in 19c. anthropology and ethnography as "specifying the yellow or Mongoloid type of mankind" [Century Dictionary].

xenogamy.x:
in botany, "cross-fertilization, fertilization by pollen from a different plant of the same species," 1877, from xeno- "strange, foreign" + -gamy "fertilization." Related: Xenogamous.
Introduced in German by Anton Kerner von Marilaun, whose book appeared in English as "Flowers and their Unbidden Guests," as a term in his descriptive system, explained in a footnote:
 I understand by autogamy the fecundation of a flower by the pollen from the androecium of the same flower ; by geitonogamy, the fecundation of a flower by pollen from other flowers on the same plant ; by xenogamy the fecundation of a flower by pollen from other plants. Geitonogamy and xenogamy may be classed together under the name allogamy. Such terms as "self-fertilisation" are to be avoided on account of their excessive indefiniteness.

xenelasia.x: "prevention of aliens from settling in Sparta," which had a law prohibiting strangers from residing there without permission, Greek, literally "expulsion of foreigners," from xenelatein "to expel foreigners," from xenos "stranger" (see xeno-) + elatos, verbal adjective of elaunein "drive, drive away, beat out," which is of uncertain origin; according to Watkins from an extended form of the PIE base *ele- "to go." Sometimes Englished as xenelasy (1836).

xenophile.x: "one attracted to foreign things or people," 1922, from xeno- "foreign, strange" + -phile.

xenophobe.x: "xenophobic person," 1897; see xenophobia. A noun formed classically from it. As an adjective by 1908.

xerophagy.x: "habit of living on dry food," especially as a form of fasting or abstinence in the early Church, 1650s, from xero- "dry" + -phagy "eating" (see -phagous). Typically a diet of bread, herbs, salt, and water.

xerophyte.x: "plant adapted to a dry climate or habitat," 1897, from xero- "dry" + Greek phyton "a plant" (see phyto-).
